mainEntity.name:
Common Causes of Pulp Damage


  Deep decay: When a cavity progresses beyond the enamel and dentine, bacteria can reach the pulp and cause infection
  Cracked or chipped teeth: A fracture can expose the pulp to bacteria, even if the crack isn't visible
  Repeated dental procedures: Multiple treatments on the same tooth can stress the pulp over time
  Trauma or injury: A blow to the mouth can damage the pulp, sometimes without any visible signs on the tooth's surface
  Large fillings: Extensive restorations may leave little protection for the underlying pulp


Signs You May Need Treatment

acceptedAnswer.text: Watch for these symptoms, which may indicate pulp damage:
Your dentist will first examine your tooth and take X-rays to assess the extent of infection and see the shape of the root canals. This helps plan the most effective treatment approach.

Before treatment begins, your dentist will administer a local anaesthetic to numb the area around the affected tooth. Most patients feel little to no discomfort during the procedure — typically just some pressure or movement. If you experience discomfort at any point, your dentist can adjust the anaesthesia.

Once you're comfortable, your dentist will place a protective sheet (rubber dam) around the tooth to keep it clean and dry. A small opening is then made in the crown of the tooth to access the pulp chamber.
Using specialised instruments, your dentist carefully removes the infected or damaged pulp tissue from the pulp chamber and root canals. This step eliminates the source of infection and pain.
The empty canals are thoroughly cleaned, disinfected, and shaped to prepare them for filling. Your dentist may use irrigation solutions to flush away debris and bacteria.
The cleaned canals are filled with a biocompatible material called gutta-percha, which is placed with adhesive cement to ensure a complete seal. This prevents bacteria from re-entering.

After the root canal is complete, your tooth will need a permanent restoration—usually a crown—to protect it and restore full function. A tooth that has had root canal treatment can become more brittle, so a crown provides essential reinforcement.

Today's dental techniques and anaesthetics have greatly improved the root canal experience. Your dentist will administer local anaesthetic before beginning, and many patients report that the procedure feels similar to having a standard filling.

mainEntity.name:
What You Might Feel


  During treatment: Most patients feel pressure and movement but no sharp pain. If you feel discomfort at any point, let your dentist know—additional anaesthetic can be provided
  After treatment: Some tenderness or mild discomfort is normal for a few days. This typically responds well to over-the-counter pain relief


Pain From Infection vs Treatment

acceptedAnswer.text: It's worth noting that the pain people associate with root canals often comes from the infection itself—not the treatment. In fact, most patients feel significant relief once the infected tissue is removed. The procedure is the solution to pain, not the cause.

mainEntity.name:
Managing Discomfort


  Some tenderness is normal for a few days—this usually improves steadily
  Over-the-counter pain relievers like paracetamol or ibuprofen can help manage any discomfort
  Avoid chewing on the treated side until any temporary filling is replaced with a permanent restoration


Eating and Drinking


  Wait until the numbness wears off completely before eating to avoid accidentally biting your cheek or tongue
  Stick to soft foods for the first day or two
  Avoid very hot or cold foods if you experience sensitivity
  Don't chew directly on the treated tooth until it has been fully restored with a crown


Oral Hygiene


  Continue brushing and flossing as normal, being gentle around the treated area
  Rinse gently with warm salt water if recommended by your dentist
  Attend your follow-up appointment to have the permanent restoration placed


When to Contact Your Dentist

If you're experiencing any of the symptoms mentioned above, our friendly team at Smile Dentist is here to help. We'll assess your situation and discuss all your options in a comfortable, pressure-free environment.

mainEntity.name: How long does a root canal take?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most root canal treatments take between 60 to 90 minutes, though this can vary depending on the tooth's complexity. Front teeth are often quicker to treat than molars, which have multiple roots.

mainEntity.name: How much does root canal treatment cost in the UK?

acceptedAnswer.text: Costs vary depending on whether you're treated privately or on the NHS, and which tooth requires treatment. Your dentist will provide a clear breakdown of costs before treatment begins.

mainEntity.name: Can I drive home after a root canal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Yes, in most cases. Root canal treatment uses local anaesthetic, which numbs only the treatment area. You should be fine to drive once the numbness begins to wear off.

mainEntity.name: How long does it take to recover from a root canal?

acceptedAnswer.text: Most patients feel back to normal within a few days. Any tenderness typically subsides within a week. You'll need a follow-up appointment for your permanent restoration.

mainEntity.name: Is a crown always needed after root canal treatment?

acceptedAnswer.text: In most cases, yes—especially for back teeth. A crown protects the tooth from fracture and restores its strength. Your dentist will advise on the best restoration for your specific situation.

mainEntity.name: What happens if I don't get a root canal when I need one?

acceptedAnswer.text: Without treatment, the infection can spread, potentially leading to an abscess, bone loss, or the need for extraction. In rare cases, untreated dental infections can affect overall health.

While root canal treatment is a well-established procedure with generally favourable outcomes, occasionally a tooth may not heal as expected or develop new problems. If this occurs, retreatment or other options may help preserve the tooth.
